newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam trial signals determination against graft.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam trial signals determination against graft.

text.p: Vietnam's state-controlled media splashed details of a major fraud trial across front pages on Thursday as the communist government stepped up a propaganda battle against worsening corruption.
Newspapers carried photos of the eight grim-faced trial defendants, dressed in prison clothes and standing before a court bench in Ho Chi Minh City.
The reports detailed the means by which Tran Xuan Hoa, director of a rice and fertiliser trading firm, and others are said to have duped the state out of more than $12 million and a quantity of gold.
Hoa, considered the ringleader, fled across the border into Cambodia in 1994 and was not present at the trial, which is expected to last until Saturday.

Corruption, which is endemic, has emerged as a major problem for Vietnam in recent months. Although the issue is not new, it has acquired political overtones in the wake of a Communist Party congress last June.

Conservatives argue that graft has worsened with economic reforms introduced in the late 1980s. Others say it is a reflection of more fundamental problems arising, in part, from an unwieldy government bureaucracy.
Despite growing wealth, Vietnam is still one of the world's poorest countries. But it has acquired an unenviable reputation as being one of the most graft-ridden nations in Asia.
State media has billed the trial as the biggest-ever of its kind in Vietnam, but an even higher-profile case involving Ho Chi Minh City firm Tamexco is set to begin within a week.
The case has involved investigations into the activities of top bankers and senior officials, sending shockwaves across the establishment even before coming to court.
Among those implicated are several people with connections to some of the most powerful figures in Vietnam.
